(1) a simulated handwriting-recog- nition system and a simulated speech-recog- nization system can be used for editing documents, and (2) editing with these systems was much faster than with a full- screen text editor.
editing is faster with a simulated handwriting recognition system than with a simulated speech recognition system, and that editing is faster than with a full screen text editor.
the simulated handwriting-recognition and simulated speech-recognition systems provided better support than a full-screen text-editor for revising marked-up manuscripts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a text-editing system that will be based on the use of speech-recognition and handwriting-recognition technologies.
the design of text-editing systems that are more responsive to the needs of users.
the design of text editors that are more responsive to the needs of the user.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the use of handwriting-recognition systems, speech-recognition systems and text editors is not yet well enough understood to permit the selection of the best system for a given task.

the results of the study are consistent with the hypothesis that the external-feedback mechanisms of the simulated handwriting- and speech-recognition workstations, which are not present in a conventional text editor, can be important in supporting the cognitive activities of editing text.

the use of a text editor, a handwriting-recognition system, and a speech-recognition system for revising documents is a function of the type of editing to be done, the nature of the document, and the skill of the editor.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the external-feedback characteristics of a system, rather than its internal characteristics, may be the most important determiner of how effectively it is used.
a good text editor should be designed to support the way the user thinks, not the way the computer thinks.
the more a system resembles the user's preferred mode of input, the more likely it is that the system will be useful for the user.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the design of text editors must take into account how the user will interact with the document, not just how the user will edit the document.
text editors can be made more productive if they are designed to support the cognitive activities that typists engage in when revising.
the way in which a user interacts with a computer system can have a profound influence on the user's performance.
